title: Choose the visual world for the DocsForge panel
question: The roll assigned Progressive Flight Strip. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Progressive Flight Strip
options.lineage: air traffic control progressive strip bays
options.thesis: Every fetch is a strip in a bay, and the tint of the strip is what kind of source it is.
options.viewport: A dark bay rail down the left holds one tinted strip per source, each printed with its type, byte count and status; the selected strip's Markdown fills the paper pane at right, with copy and download at its foot.
options.risk: A bay of strips becomes decorative chrome the moment the tints stop actually classifying anything.

options.label: Teletext Service
options.thesis: Documentation as a broadcast index: three-digit pages, not sections.
options.case: Fuses well on tables, loading counters and status flags, but its sacred 40x24 cell grid scales rather than reflows, which a narrow docked panel cannot survive.

options.label: HyperCard Stack
options.thesis: The tool for reading the docs is the tool for making the document.
options.case: Conceptually the closest fit of the three, since reading and authoring really are one act here; fuses poorly because one-bit dither and fixed-proportion cards fight dense API tables and long code blocks.

options.label: Miura Deployable Sheet
options.thesis: One URL is a packet; one pull deploys it into a vast precise field.
options.case: The packet-to-field unfold is an apt metaphor for what a fetch does; fuses poorly because a parallelogram crease grid ruling every block is hostile to reading long Markdown.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A centred chat column with bubbles and a rendered Markdown reply, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: Conversation down the middle, composer pinned at the bottom, each reply rendered with copy and download actions.
canonCard.risk: It is what every AI chat surface already looks like, including the one currently in this repo.
